cells.tense: You are holding what needs holding, and the holding is not costing you the shape of yourself.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: When someone brings you their weight, feel it with them as you listen, not only about them. Stay where you stand and say your own side as plainly as you take in theirs.
cells.core:
Whatever you're carrying sits within reach of your own way of being, and it doesn't flatten it. You can take the weight of a bad week or a heavy season and still be recognizably yourself in it — the worry, the dry humour, the way you sound when you're fine. That's the difference between steadying and hardening. The harder version will come, and you'll know it because nobody can get near what's in your grip.

There's a way of holding that doesn't do that. When someone brings their weight to you, feel it with them for a minute. Stay next to it, keep your own two feet where they are, and don't take it out of their hands. Mostly that's a matter of not rushing to fix anything. Your feeling stays yours while theirs touches it.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy and still be yourself in it.
cells.verb: bearing what must be borne without hardening or breaking
cells.place: in the place where you become what you already are

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of the load that has not landed yet, and the brace has gotten heavier than the load.
cells.act: put it in proportion, not in punishment
cells.ask: Take whatever you're white-knuckling right now and say out loud what the fair share of it is to carry. Set the rest down, and don't pay yourself back for the trouble.
cells.core:
You can feel the load before it lands. Something in you gets ready early — carries next month's problem in this month's shoulders, decides how it's going to go before it's gone anywhere. The strength is real and it's doing a lot; it's also gone past the work. What you're bracing for is a version of the situation the situation hasn't asked for.

You can tell weight from worry when you stop moving. Look at whatever you're holding too tightly, and see what the fair size of it is. Not what would punish you for struggling — what proportion actually calls for. Hold that, put the rest down. What you're owed and what you owe can flow both ways again once the extra isn't in your hands. You'll move further than you did while bracing.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying a storm that hasn't been forecast yet.

cells.tense: You stood at a door and the room behind you has already changed shape.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Set down on purpose what you're still gripping that no longer needs holding — not by losing it, by setting it down. Then let your hands stay empty before anything new gets picked up.
cells.core:
There's a spot where you used to hold something — a role, a version of yourself, a load nobody asked you to drop. It's still there in your grip, but the thing itself is gone, and the stance has stayed. When pressure comes now, the part that used to bear it feels too far away to reach, and you can watch yourself waiting for permission you can't give.

Letting go is the opposite of giving up here. Not because what happened was nothing, but because there's nothing left to hold. Choose the old guilt, the kept promise nobody's asking about, and set it down deliberately. Sit with empty hands. What's yours will come back and pick itself up.
cells.sheetLine: You're still gripping something the room already let go of.

cells.tense: You keep doing what keeps everyone upright, and your account of it has you standing around watching.
cells.act: let yourself want it, plainly, to yourself
cells.ask: Before sleep tonight, put into words something you actually want for yourself, not for anyone else, and hold it there without explaining it, shrinking it, or justifying it.
cells.core:
There's a strength holding everything steady that nobody has named, and you're sure it's just how things are. You stood through the difficult stretch — you're standing through it — and the version of events has you as the one who happened to be nearby. People lean on it; you don't count it. What you carry looks like terrain to you, not work you're doing.

There's an older, simpler thing under all that, and it's still yours. Before you were the one holding it all, you were someone who wanted things — for their own sake, not because someone else needed them. Let that person want something again, no one watching. You hold best when you're pointed somewhere too.
cells.sheetLine: The strength here is yours, and your story files it under furniture.
